citations.quote: Let $[a,b]$ be a bounded interval and let $a\le t_1<\cdots<t_r\le b$ with $r\ge2$. A natural cubic spline with knots $t_1,\ldots,t_r$ is a $C^2$ function on $[a,b]$ that is a polynomial of degree at most three on every $[t_j,t_{j+1}]$, has second derivative zero at $t_1$ and $t_r$, and is extended linearly on $[a,t_1]$ and $[t_r,b]$ when those intervals are nonempty. The knots $t_j$ are the distinct breakpoints; repeated observations at the same input do not create additional knots.

derivations.claim: Put $h_i=x_{i+1}-x_i$ and $d_i=(y_{i+1}-y_i)/h_i$. For $r=2$ there are no interior second derivatives to solve. For $r\ge3$, let $A$ be the $(r-2)\times(r-2)$ symmetric tridiagonal matrix with diagonal entry $2(h_{i-1}+h_i)$ in row $i$ and adjacent off-diagonal entries $h_i$. For a nonzero vector $v=(v_2,\ldots,v_{r-1})$, using $2v_iv_{i+1}\ge-v_i^2-v_{i+1}^2$ gives $v^TAv\ge\sum_{i=2}^{r-1}(h_{i-1}+h_i)v_i^2>0.$ Thus $A$ is positive definite and invertible, so the displayed system has exactly one solution $M_2,\ldots,M_{r-1}$.

On each interval define the displayed cubic. Direct substitution gives its endpoint values and second derivatives. Its left and right endpoint slopes are respectively d_i−M_i h_i/3−M_{i+1}h_i/6 and d_i+M_i h_i/6+M_{i+1}h_i/3. Equating the right slope from s_{i−1} and the left slope from s_i gives the tridiagonal equation. Hence the pieces join C^1; their second derivatives are linear with the same nodal values, so they join C^2. At the extreme knots M_1=M_r=0, so adjoining the tangent line gives the required linear tails and preserves C^2. For r=2, the formula is the straight line between the two values.

Any natural cubic interpolant has nodal second derivatives with $M_1=M_r=0$. Equality of its adjacent endpoint slopes forces the displayed tridiagonal equations, so by step 1.1 its nodal second derivatives equal the constructed ones. On each interval, the difference from $s_i$ is a cubic with zero second derivative at both endpoints; its second derivative is affine and therefore zero throughout, so the difference is affine and vanishes at both endpoint values. It is identically zero. Thus the interpolant is unique.

Let $p\in\mathbb N_0$, $n\ge p+1$, and $a<b$. A clamped knot vector is a nondecreasing finite sequence
$$\xi_1=\cdots=\xi_{p+1}=a<\xi_{p+2}\le\cdots\le\xi_n<\xi_{n+1}=\cdots=\xi_{n+p+1}=b,$$
with $\xi_j<\xi_{j+p+1}$ for every $1\le j\le n$. Empty interior ranges are omitted. The multiplicity $\mu(\eta)$ of an interior knot $\eta$ is its number of occurrences among $\xi_{p+2},\ldots,\xi_n$.

Write $\mathcal P_p$ for the real polynomials of degree at most $p$. The degree-$p$ spline space $S_{p,\xi}$ consists of functions that restrict to a member of $\mathcal P_p$ on each nonempty knot interval and whose derivatives through order $p-\mu(\eta)$ agree across each interior knot $\eta$. The convention $C^{-1}$ means that no matching condition is imposed. For this piecewise definition, take knot cells left-closed and right-open; at a knot with no matching condition, the value is the one from the cell on its right, and at $b$ use the left limit. Thus the function value at a discontinuous knot is specified.

For each degree $d\in\{0,\ldots,p\}$, the functions $B_{j,d,\xi}$ are indexed by $1\le j\le n+p-d$. Set
$$B_{j,0,\xi}(x)=\mathbf 1_{[\xi_j,\xi_{j+1})}(x),\qquad 1\le j\le n+p.$$
For $1\le d\le p$ and $1\le j\le n+p-d$, define recursively
$$B_{j,d,\xi}(x)=\frac{x-\xi_j}{\xi_{j+d}-\xi_j}B_{j,d-1,\xi}(x)+\frac{\xi_{j+d+1}-x}{\xi_{j+d+1}-\xi_{j+1}}B_{j+1,d-1,\xi}(x),$$
where a term with zero denominator is defined to be zero. For every degree $d$ and every allowed index $j$, set $B_{j,d,\xi}(b)$ equal to its left limit. In particular, the degree-$p$ family has indices $1\le j\le n$. Its basis and regularity properties are proved in [[thm-spline-polynomial-reproduction]].

derivations.claim: For $p=0$, support, piecewise degree, and nonnegativity follow from the indicator definition in [F1]. Inductively, each degree-$p$ term is a lower-degree spline multiplied by an affine factor; on the lower-degree spline's support that factor is nonnegative, and the two supports lie inside $[\xi_j, \xi_{j+p+1}]$. Thus support, degree at most $p$, and nonnegativity hold for every $p$.

Let the distinct interior knots be $\eta_1<\cdots<\eta_s$ with multiplicities $\mu_1,\ldots,\mu_s$. For $k\ge1$ set $u_{r,k}(x)=(x-\eta_r)^k\mathbf1_{[\eta_r,\infty)}(x)$ and set $u_{r,0}(x)=\mathbf1_{[\eta_r,\infty)}(x)$; the value at $\eta_r$ follows the right-cell convention of [F1]. The functions $1,x,\ldots,x^p$ together with $u_{r,k}$ for $p-\mu_r+1\le k\le p$ span $S_{p,\xi}$: start with the polynomial on the first interval, then at each knot the difference of adjacent pieces has its derivatives through $p-\mu_r$ equal to zero, so it is a linear combination of the listed powers, including the right-continuous step when $\mu_r=p+1$. They are independent because restriction to successive knot intervals first forces the initial polynomial coefficients, then each new knot's coefficients, to vanish. Thus $\dim S_{p,\xi}=p+1+\sum_r\mu_r=n$.

Define $\psi_{j,0}(y)=1$ and $\psi_{j,d}(y)=\prod_{r=1}^{d}(y-\xi_{j+r})$. When $\xi_{j+d}>\xi_j$, factoring $\psi_{j,d-1}$ gives $(y-x)\psi_{j,d-1}(y)=\frac{x-\xi_j}{\xi_{j+d}-\xi_j}\psi_{j,d}(y)+\frac{\xi_{j+d}-x}{\xi_{j+d}-\xi_j}\psi_{j-1,d}(y)$. Fix a nonempty cell $[\xi_m,\xi_{m+1})$. At degree zero its sole nonzero indicator is $B_{m,0,\xi}$, so the local identity holds. Inductively, the degree-$(d-1)$ local sum has indices $m-d+1\le j\le m$. For every such index, $\xi_j\le\xi_m<\xi_{m+1}\le\xi_{j+d}$, so the displayed identity has a strictly positive denominator. Multiply that local sum by $y-x$, apply the identity, and regroup with [F1]. The two extra lower-degree functions $B_{m-d,d-1,\xi}$ and $B_{m+1,d-1,\xi}$ vanish on the cell by support, even when their supports are empty; their recurrence terms are zero under [F1]. Thus $(y-x)^d=\sum_{i=m-d}^{m}\psi_{i,d}(y)B_{i,d,\xi}(x)$ for $0\le d\le p$, and in particular for $d=p$.

Differentiate the identity in step 2.1 exactly $p-k$ times in $y$ and set $y=0$, for each $0\le k\le p$. Since $\frac{d^{p-k}}{dy^{p-k}}(y-x)^p|_{y=0}=\frac{p!}{k!}(-x)^k$, this yields $x^k=\sum_{i=m-p}^{m}\left[(-1)^k\frac{k!}{p!}\psi_{i, p}^{(p-k)}(0)\right]B_{i,p,\xi}(x).$ The coefficients do not depend on $m$, so this is a single expansion valid on every knot interval. Linear combination proves reproduction of every member of $\mathcal P_p$; taking left limits extends the expansion to $b$.

Fix an open nonempty knot interval $(\xi_m,\xi_{m+1})$ and $p\ge1$. The $p+1$ dual polynomials $\psi_{i,p}$, $m-p\le i\le m$, form a basis of $\mathcal P_p$ in $y$: differentiating the identity of step 2.1 in $x$ at an interior point $x_0$ shows that their span contains $(y-x_0)^k$ for every $0\le k\le p$. For $m-p+1\le i\le m$, the span $\xi_{i+p}-\xi_i$ is strictly positive and factoring gives $\psi_{i,p}-\psi_{i-1,p}=-(\xi_{i+p}-\xi_i)\psi_{i,p-1}$. Differentiate the degree-$p$ local identity in $x$ and use the degree-$(p-1)$ identity and this difference formula to obtain $\sum_{i=m-p}^{m}B'_{i,p,\xi}\psi_{i,p}=p\sum_{i=m-p+1}^{m}\frac{B_{i,p-1,\xi}}{\xi_{i+p}-\xi_i}(\psi_{i,p}-\psi_{i-1,p})$. Comparison in the dual basis yields $B'_{j,p,\xi}=p\left(\frac{B_{j,p-1,\xi}}{\xi_{j+p}-\xi_j}-\frac{B_{j+1,p-1,\xi}}{\xi_{j+p+1}-\xi_{j+1}}\right)$ on this interval. The boundary lower-degree terms vanish by support; any zero denominator corresponds to an identically zero lower-degree spline and its term is zero. For indices outside the active range both sides vanish by support.

Taking $k=0$ in step 3.1 gives $\sum_{i=m-p}^{m}B_{i,p,\xi}(x)=1$. Step 3.1 also shows that these $p+1$ active functions span $\mathcal P_p$ on the interval. Because $\dim\mathcal P_p=p+1$, they are linearly independent there and are a local basis.

Induct on $p$. If the knot multiplicity $\mu\le p-1$, the lower-degree splines in the recurrence are continuous there by induction, so the recurrence makes $B_{j,p,\xi}$ continuous; the derivative formula then makes its derivative $C^{p-1-\mu}$, hence $B_{j,p,\xi}\in C^{p-\mu}$. If $\mu=p$, a B-spline whose support crosses the repeated knot has one nonzero piece on either side, namely $(x-\xi_j)^p/(\xi_{j+p}-\xi_j)^p$ and $(\xi_{j+p+1}-x)^p/(\xi_{j+p+1}-\xi_{j+1})^p$; both one-sided limits equal $1$, while any B-spline not crossing it has zero endpoint value there. If $\mu=p+1$, the required order is $C^{-1}$ and no matching is asserted.

The smoothness and piecewise-degree properties from steps 1.1 and 4.2 put every B-spline in $S_{p,\xi}$. If a linear combination of all $n$ B-splines is zero, then on every nonempty knot interval its active coefficients vanish by the local basis property in step 4.1. Each B-spline has a nonempty support interval by the clamped-knot hypothesis, so every coefficient occurs on at least one such interval and is zero. The B-splines are therefore $n$ independent members of the $n$-dimensional space in step 1.2, hence form its basis. The unique global expansion includes every polynomial from step 3.1.

citations.quote:
The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> ([[def-choice-function]]).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

Assume Countable Choice. Let $\Omega\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be open with
$n\ge1$, $k\in\mathbb N_0$, $1\le p\le\infty$, and
$\mathbb K\in\{\mathbb R,\mathbb C\}$. Write
$$\mathcal A_k=\{\alpha\in\mathbb N_0^n:|\alpha|\le k\}.$$
This is a finite nonempty set: every coordinate of such an $\alpha$ lies in
$\{0,\ldots,k\}$, and it contains the zero multi-index.

The real and complex $L^p$ classes use the conventions in
[[def-l-p-space-as-a-quotient-by-null-functions]] and
[[def-complex-lp-and-euclidean-test-function-conventions]]. Their quotient
norm values are supplied by
[[thm-the-l-p-norm-descends-to-the-quotient-and-makes-l-p-a-normed-space]]
for real scalars and
[[thm-complex-holder-minkowski-and-the-quotient-norm]] for complex scalars.

Define $W^{k,p}(\Omega;\mathbb K)$ to be the set of classes
$u\in L^p(\Omega;\mathbb K)$ such that, for every $\alpha\in\mathcal A_k$,
there is an $L^p(\Omega;\mathbb K)$ class with a locally integrable
representative $v_\alpha$ satisfying
$$\int_\Omega u\,D^\alpha\varphi\,dx =(-1)^{|\alpha|}\int_\Omega v_\alpha\varphi\,dx \qquad\text{for every }\varphi\in C_c^\infty(\Omega).$$
Here the weak derivative is the one in
[[def-weak-derivative-of-a-locally-integrable-function]]. Under
[[def-countable-choice]], local integrability of $L^p$ representatives and
invariance under null-set changes follow from
[[lem-weak-derivative-is-independent-of-lp-representatives]], while
[[lem-weak-derivatives-are-unique-almost-everywhere]] gives uniqueness of each
locally integrable derivative class. Thus this condition is a condition on the
$L^p$ class $u$, and each resulting derivative determines one $L^p$ class,
denoted $D^\alpha u$. The test pairing is bilinear, without conjugation.

For the zero multi-index, set $D^0u=u$. Since $\mathcal A_0=\{0\}$,
$$W^{0,p}(\Omega;\mathbb K)=L^p(\Omega;\mathbb K).$$
The Sobolev norm expression is
$$\|u\|_{W^{k,p}(\Omega)}= \begin{cases} \left(\displaystyle\sum_{\alpha\in\mathcal A_k} \|D^\alpha u\|_{L^p(\Omega)}^p\right)^{1/p},&1\le p<\infty,\\[1ex] \displaystyle\max_{\alpha\in\mathcal A_k} \|D^\alpha u\|_{L^\infty(\Omega)},&p=\infty. \end{cases}$$
The formula is finite because each derivative class belongs to $L^p$ and
$\mathcal A_k$ is finite; at $k=0$ it reduces to the $L^p$ norm expression.
The finite maximum is defined because $\mathcal A_k$ is nonempty. The norm
axioms for this expression are a separate assertion from this definition.

For open $U\subseteq\Omega$ with $\overline U$ compact and contained in
$\Omega$, the notation $W^{k,p}_{\mathrm{loc}}(\Omega;\mathbb K)$ means that
the restriction of the class belongs to $W^{k,p}(U;\mathbb K)$ for every such
$U$.

If $\Omega=\varnothing$, the $L^p$ space and every $W^{k,p}$ space contain
only the zero class, and the displayed norm expression is zero.

Assume the Axiom of Choice for the ACL and absolutely-continuous
fundamental-theorem interfaces. Let $I\subseteq\mathbb R$ be a nonempty open
interval, let $1\le p\le\infty$, let $\mathbb K\in\{\mathbb R,\mathbb C\}$,
and let $u\in W^{1,p}(I;\mathbb K)$, with weak derivative class $Du$. Then
there is exactly one continuous representative $u^*$ of the class of $u$ on
$I$ that is locally absolutely continuous, that is, absolutely continuous on
every compact interval contained in $I$, and satisfies
$$u^*(x)-u^*(y)=\int_y^xDu(t)\,dt\qquad\text{for every }x,y\in I,$$
where for $x<y$ the right-hand side denotes $-\int_x^yDu$, equivalently
$u^*(y)-u^*(x)=\int_x^yDu$ whenever $x\le y$.

If $I=(a,b)$ has finite endpoints, then $Du\in L^1(a,b)$, the representative
$u^*$ extends uniquely to an absolutely continuous function on $[a,b]$, and
the extension satisfies
$$u^*(x)=u^*(a)+\int_a^xDu(t)\,dt\qquad\text{for every }x\in[a,b].$$

The scalar field is arbitrary, $p=1$ and $p=\infty$ are included, and the
one-dimensional interval may be bounded or unbounded. The Axiom of Choice is
used only through the Countable-Choice and Dependent-Choice hypotheses of the
cited characterisation, fundamental-theorem and completeness interfaces.

Let $r\ge2$, $a\le x_1<\cdots<x_r\le b$, and $y_1,\ldots,y_r\in\mathbb R$. There is exactly one natural cubic spline $s$ on $[a,b]$ with $s(x_i)=y_i$ for each $i$. On each interval $[x_i,x_{i+1}]$ it is the cubic with endpoint values $y_i,y_{i+1}$ and endpoint second derivatives $M_i,M_{i+1}$, where $M_1=M_r=0$ and the interior values solve the positive-definite tridiagonal system
$$h_{i-1}M_{i-1}+2(h_{i-1}+h_i)M_i+h_iM_{i+1}=6\left(\frac{y_{i+1}-y_i}{h_i}-\frac{y_i-y_{i-1}}{h_{i-1}}\right),\quad 2\le i\le r-1,$$
with $h_i=x_{i+1}-x_i>0$. The interpolant is linear outside $[x_1,x_r]$.

Assume AC. Let $[a,b]$ be a bounded interval, let $(x_i,y_i)_{i=1}^n\in([a,b]\times\mathbb R)^n$, assume at least two distinct input values, and let $\lambda>0$. For $g\in W^{2,2}(a,b)$ use its unique continuous representative on $[a,b]$ supplied by the one-dimensional Sobolev representative theorem. The natural cubic smoothing spline is the unique minimizer, whose existence and uniqueness are proved in [[thm-natural-cubic-smoothing-spline-exists-uniquely]], of
$$J(g)=\sum_{i=1}^n(y_i-g(x_i))^2+\lambda\int_a^b|D^2g(t)|^2\,dt.$$

The requirement of two distinct inputs is essential. The penalty is the squared $L^2$ norm of the second weak derivative. The data term includes every observation, including repeated inputs; only the spline knots are the distinct input values, as in [[def-natural-cubic-spline]].

In ZF, assume the Axiom of Choice. Then the Axiom of Countable Choice holds.
Moreover, if $R\subseteq X\times X$ is a serial relation on a nonempty set
$X$ and $a\in X$, there is a sequence $(x_n)_{n\in\mathbb N}$ such that
$x_0=a$ and $x_nRx_{n+1}$ for every $n$. Thus AC supplies the
prescribed-initial-point form of Dependent Choice.

derivations.claim: Let $g\in W^{2,2}(a,b)$ and use the continuous representative in [F2] for $g$ and $g'$. The Countable Choice convention in [F1] and the choice hypotheses for [F2] are available by [F5] and [A1]. Interpolate the values $g(t_j)$ by the natural cubic $s$ from [F3], and put $h=g-s$. Then $h(t_j)=0$ for every $j$. On each interval between distinct knots, $s'''$ is constant; on the two linear tails, $s''=s'''=0$.

The natural spline with knots $t_1,\ldots,t_r$ is uniquely determined by its nodal vector $z=(s(t_1),\ldots,s(t_r))\in\mathbb R^r$ by [F3]. The tridiagonal system in the interpolation proof is linear in its data, and the interval formula is linear in the nodal values and second derivatives; hence $z\mapsto s_z''$ is linear into the finite-dimensional space of piecewise-linear functions. Therefore $R(z)=\int|s_z''|^2$ is a finite nonnegative quadratic form. In these coordinates $J(s)=\sum_j\sum_{i:x_i=t_j}(y_i-z_j)^2+\lambda R(z)$. The data term has positive-definite diagonal quadratic part because every $t_j$ occurs at least once. Adding the nonnegative quadratic form $\lambda R$ leaves a positive-definite quadratic objective, which has a unique minimizer by completing the square.

On each knot interval, the product $s''h'$ is absolutely continuous, so the fundamental theorem of calculus gives $\int s''h''=[s''h']-\int s'''h'$. Summing over the intervals, the interior boundary terms cancel because $s''$ and $h'$ are continuous. At each outer endpoint, $s''=0$ either on a linear tail or by the natural condition when that endpoint is a knot. The remaining terms are $-s'''|_{(t_j,t_{j+1})}(h(t_{j+1})-h(t_j))=0$. Thus $\int_a^b s''h''=0$.

Since $g=s+h$, expanding the square and applying step 2.1 yields $\int_a^b|g''|^2=\int_a^b|s''|^2+\int_a^b|h''|^2.$ Also $s(x_i)=g(x_i)$ for every observed input, so their data residual terms agree. Therefore $J(g)=J(s)+\lambda\int_a^b|h''|^2\ge J(s)$, with equality only if $h''=0$ almost everywhere.

Let $s_*$ be this finite-dimensional minimizer. Step 3.1 shows $J(g)\ge J(s_*)$ for every $g\in W^{2,2}$. If equality holds, then $h''=0$ almost everywhere, so by [F2] $h$ is affine; its zero values at the two distinct knots $t_1,t_r$ force $h=0$. Thus $s_*$ is the unique minimizer over the full Sobolev class, and its natural cubic form and linear tails are those of [F3].

The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> ([[def-choice-function]]).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

Assume Countable Choice. Let $\Omega\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be open with
$n\ge1$, $k\in\mathbb N_0$, $1\le p\le\infty$, and
$\mathbb K\in\{\mathbb R,\mathbb C\}$. Write
$$\mathcal A_k=\{\alpha\in\mathbb N_0^n:|\alpha|\le k\}.$$
This is a finite nonempty set: every coordinate of such an $\alpha$ lies in
$\{0,\ldots,k\}$, and it contains the zero multi-index.

The real and complex $L^p$ classes use the conventions in
[[def-l-p-space-as-a-quotient-by-null-functions]] and
[[def-complex-lp-and-euclidean-test-function-conventions]]. Their quotient
norm values are supplied by
[[thm-the-l-p-norm-descends-to-the-quotient-and-makes-l-p-a-normed-space]]
for real scalars and
[[thm-complex-holder-minkowski-and-the-quotient-norm]] for complex scalars.

Define $W^{k,p}(\Omega;\mathbb K)$ to be the set of classes
$u\in L^p(\Omega;\mathbb K)$ such that, for every $\alpha\in\mathcal A_k$,
there is an $L^p(\Omega;\mathbb K)$ class with a locally integrable
representative $v_\alpha$ satisfying
$$\int_\Omega u\,D^\alpha\varphi\,dx =(-1)^{|\alpha|}\int_\Omega v_\alpha\varphi\,dx \qquad\text{for every }\varphi\in C_c^\infty(\Omega).$$
Here the weak derivative is the one in
[[def-weak-derivative-of-a-locally-integrable-function]]. Under
[[def-countable-choice]], local integrability of $L^p$ representatives and
invariance under null-set changes follow from
[[lem-weak-derivative-is-independent-of-lp-representatives]], while
[[lem-weak-derivatives-are-unique-almost-everywhere]] gives uniqueness of each
locally integrable derivative class. Thus this condition is a condition on the
$L^p$ class $u$, and each resulting derivative determines one $L^p$ class,
denoted $D^\alpha u$. The test pairing is bilinear, without conjugation.

For the zero multi-index, set $D^0u=u$. Since $\mathcal A_0=\{0\}$,
$$W^{0,p}(\Omega;\mathbb K)=L^p(\Omega;\mathbb K).$$
The Sobolev norm expression is
$$\|u\|_{W^{k,p}(\Omega)}= \begin{cases} \left(\displaystyle\sum_{\alpha\in\mathcal A_k} \|D^\alpha u\|_{L^p(\Omega)}^p\right)^{1/p},&1\le p<\infty,\\[1ex] \displaystyle\max_{\alpha\in\mathcal A_k} \|D^\alpha u\|_{L^\infty(\Omega)},&p=\infty. \end{cases}$$
The formula is finite because each derivative class belongs to $L^p$ and
$\mathcal A_k$ is finite; at $k=0$ it reduces to the $L^p$ norm expression.
The finite maximum is defined because $\mathcal A_k$ is nonempty. The norm
axioms for this expression are a separate assertion from this definition.

For open $U\subseteq\Omega$ with $\overline U$ compact and contained in
$\Omega$, the notation $W^{k,p}_{\mathrm{loc}}(\Omega;\mathbb K)$ means that
the restriction of the class belongs to $W^{k,p}(U;\mathbb K)$ for every such
$U$.

If $\Omega=\varnothing$, the $L^p$ space and every $W^{k,p}$ space contain
only the zero class, and the displayed norm expression is zero.

Assume the Axiom of Choice for the ACL and absolutely-continuous
fundamental-theorem interfaces. Let $I\subseteq\mathbb R$ be a nonempty open
interval, let $1\le p\le\infty$, let $\mathbb K\in\{\mathbb R,\mathbb C\}$,
and let $u\in W^{1,p}(I;\mathbb K)$, with weak derivative class $Du$. Then
there is exactly one continuous representative $u^*$ of the class of $u$ on
$I$ that is locally absolutely continuous, that is, absolutely continuous on
every compact interval contained in $I$, and satisfies
$$u^*(x)-u^*(y)=\int_y^xDu(t)\,dt\qquad\text{for every }x,y\in I,$$
where for $x<y$ the right-hand side denotes $-\int_x^yDu$, equivalently
$u^*(y)-u^*(x)=\int_x^yDu$ whenever $x\le y$.

If $I=(a,b)$ has finite endpoints, then $Du\in L^1(a,b)$, the representative
$u^*$ extends uniquely to an absolutely continuous function on $[a,b]$, and
the extension satisfies
$$u^*(x)=u^*(a)+\int_a^xDu(t)\,dt\qquad\text{for every }x\in[a,b].$$

The scalar field is arbitrary, $p=1$ and $p=\infty$ are included, and the
one-dimensional interval may be bounded or unbounded. The Axiom of Choice is
used only through the Countable-Choice and Dependent-Choice hypotheses of the
cited characterisation, fundamental-theorem and completeness interfaces.

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ be a measure space, let $p,q\in[1,\infty]$ be
conjugate exponents, and let $f,g$ be measurable real-valued functions.

1. If $1\le p<\infty$ and $q<\infty$ with $f\in\mathcal L^p(\mu)$ and
   $g\in\mathcal L^q(\mu)$, then
   $$\int |fg|\,d\mu\le\|f\|_p\|g\|_q.$$
2. If $p=1$ and $q=\infty$ with $f\in\mathcal L^1(\mu)$ and
   $g\in L^\infty(\mu)$, then
   $$\int |fg|\,d\mu\le\|f\|_1\|g\|_\infty.$$
3. If $p=\infty$ and $q=1$ with $f\in L^\infty(\mu)$ and
   $g\in\mathcal L^1(\mu)$, then
   $$\int |fg|\,d\mu\le\|f\|_\infty\|g\|_1.$$

In every case the right-hand side is finite, so $fg$ is integrable.

In ZF, assume the Axiom of Choice. Then the Axiom of Countable Choice holds.
Moreover, if $R\subseteq X\times X$ is a serial relation on a nonempty set
$X$ and $a\in X$, there is a sequence $(x_n)_{n\in\mathbb N}$ such that
$x_0=a$ and $x_nRx_{n+1}$ for every $n$. Thus AC supplies the
prescribed-initial-point form of Dependent Choice.

Fix a bounded interval $[a,b]$, a degree $p\in\mathbb N_0$, an exponent $1\le q\le\infty$, an integer $0\le l\le p$, and a nonempty family $\mathcal T$ of clamped degree-$p$ knot meshes on $[a,b]$. A **mesh-uniform bounded local quasi-interpolant** is a family of real-linear maps $Q_\xi:C([a,b];\mathbb R)\to S_{p,\xi}$, one for each $\xi\in\mathcal T$, for which there are common constants $M\in\mathbb N$ and $0\le C_Q<\infty$ such that the following hold for every $\xi\in\mathcal T$ and every nonempty cell $I_m$ of its mesh: there is a neighborhood $J_{\xi,m}\subseteq[a,b]$ containing $I_m$ and formed from at most $M$ adjacent knot cells; each point of $[a,b]$ belongs to at most $M$ of the neighborhoods $J_{\xi,m}$; (i) if $f=g$ almost everywhere on $J_{\xi,m}$, then $Q_\xi f=Q_\xi g$ almost everywhere on $I_m$; (ii) $Q_\xi v=v$ for every $v\in\mathcal P_l$; and (iii) $\|Q_\xi f\|_{L^q(I_m)}\le C_Q\|f\|_{L^q(J_{\xi,m})}$. The constants $M$ and $C_Q$ are independent of $\xi$. The derivative and continuous-representative conventions for Sobolev inputs are those of [[def-sobolev-space-wkp-and-its-norm]] and [[cor-one-dimensional-w-one-p-functions-have-absolutely-continuous-representatives]].

For a fixed mesh, the coefficient-functional formulation in Lyche–Manni–Speleers is one sufficient way to obtain these local stability and reproduction properties. Uniform constants in that construction give a family as defined here; this definition records the operator hypotheses used in the approximation proof.

derivations.claim: On any neighborhood J=[c,d], use the continuous representatives of D^j f, 0≤j≤l, supplied by [F2]. Their Sobolev-class convention [F1] and the choice hypotheses for [F2] are available under [A1] by [F5]. Repeated integration by parts for absolutely continuous functions gives the Taylor identity f(x)−T_{c,l}f(x)=1/l!∫_c^x(x−t)^lD^{l+1}f(t)dt, where T_{c,l}f(x)=Σ_{j=0}^lD^j f(c)(x−c)^j/j!. Hölder bounds the pointwise remainder and then its L^q norm by |J|^{l+1}||D^{l+1}f||_{L^q(J)}/l!, including q=1 and q=∞.

Choose c as the left endpoint of J_m and write T=T_{c,l}f. Since Q reproduces P_l, QT=T. The triangle inequality and local stability give ||f−Qf||_{L^q(I_m)}≤||f−T||_{L^q(I_m)}+||Q(f−T)||_{L^q(I_m)}≤(1+C_Q)||f−T||_{L^q(J_m)}, using I_m⊆J_m. Since |J_m|≤Mh_m by the neighborhood definition, step 1.1 gives the local estimate.

Raise the local estimates to the $q$th power and sum over the disjoint mesh cells. Each point belongs to at most $M$ neighborhoods, so $\sum_m\|D^{l+1}f\|_{L^q(J_m)}^q\le M\|D^{l+1}f\|_{L^q([a,b])}^q$. Taking the $q$th root and using $h_m\le h$ gives the stated global bound for finite $q$. For $q=\infty$, take the maximum of the local bounds; the factor $M^{1/q}$ is $1$.

On each cell, the real L^2(I) pairing is finite by Hölder and positive definite on a.e. classes. The Gram matrix of 1,x,…,x^p is positive definite because a nonzero polynomial has only finitely many roots. Solving its Gram system defines a linear cellwise projector that fixes P_p and has orthogonal residual, so Pythagoras gives L^2 contractivity. With the right-cell knot convention, these operators form a mesh-uniform local family with one-cell neighborhoods, M=1 and C_Q=1. Applying the theorem with l=s−1 gives the stated h^s bound.

boundaries.evidence: Local bounds quantify over nonempty cells; zero-length knot intervals are omitted. On a positive-length cell, Jm contains that cell and has positive h_m, permitting the Taylor remainder in step 1.1.
Steps 1.1, 2.1 and 3.1 give zero error when the derivative remainder vanishes and include every reproduced polynomial.
The order l=0 and exponent endpoints q=1 and q=infinity are covered in steps 1.1, 3.1 and 4.1.
The hypotheses allow p=l=0; step 2.1 also treats the one-cell full-multiplicity mesh.
Steps 1.1 and 3.1 use closed cell neighborhoods intersected with [a,b], including boundary cells.
Statement and A1 assume AC, and step 1.1 uses the AC-dependent one-dimensional Sobolev representatives.

boundaries.reason: Local stability and polynomial reproduction bound the Taylor residual, and controlled neighborhood overlap yields the global h-to-l-plus-one estimate.
The displayed approximation estimate is not claimed to imply locality or exact polynomial reproduction of an arbitrary operator Q.

It fixes Pp, is contractive, has one-cell neighborhoods and respects right-cell/left-b values. Checked p=0, l=0, s=p+1 and zero derivative. AC used only through stated Sobolev interfaces; no defect.

Let $n,K\ge1$, let $p_K(x)=(s_1(x),\ldots,s_K(x))^T$ be a specified $K$-dimensional spline basis on the data domain, and let $(X_i,Y_i)_{i=1}^n$ be observed real-valued data with inputs in that domain. In particular, one may specify the degree-$p$ B-spline basis $p_K(x)=(B_{1,p,\xi}(x),\ldots,B_{K,p,\xi}(x))^T$. Form the design matrix $P\in\mathbb R^{n\times K}$ with row $p_K(X_i)^T$. The **series least-squares fitted training vector** is
$$\widehat{\mathbf g}_K=\Pi_{\operatorname{col}(P)}\mathbf Y,$$
the orthogonal projection of $\mathbf Y=(Y_1,\ldots,Y_n)^T$ onto the column space of $P$. Conditional on the realized design, this is the fixed-design least-squares fitted vector of [[def-fixed-design-projection-estimator]]. Equivalently, it is $P\widehat\beta$ for any minimizer $\widehat\beta$ of $\|\mathbf Y-P\beta\|_2^2$; all such minimizers have the same fitted training vector. The training prediction loss relative to a specified target vector $\mathbf g_0=(g_0(X_1),\ldots,g_0(X_n))^T$ is $n^{-1}\|\widehat{\mathbf g}_K-\mathbf g_0\|_2^2$. This definition specifies training fitted values and makes no test-risk assertion.

Let $(\Omega,\mathcal F,\mathbb P)$ be a probability space and let
$(S,\Sigma)$ be a measurable space. A **random element** of $S$ is a measurable
map
$$X:(\Omega,\mathcal F)\to(S,\Sigma)$$
in the sense of [[def-measurable-function-between-measurable-spaces]].

When $S=\mathbb R$ and $\Sigma=\mathcal B(\mathbb R)$ from
[[def-borel-sigma-algebra]], the map $X$ is a **real random variable**.

Let $X:(\Omega,\mathcal F,\mathbb P)\to(S,\Sigma)$ be a random element. Its
**law** or **distribution** is the set function
$$\mathbb P_X:\Sigma\to[0,+\infty],\qquad \mathbb P_X(B):=\mathbb P(X^{-1}(B)).$$

Thus the law of $X$ records the probability of each measurable target set by
pulling it back to an event in the original probability space.

Let $X_i:(\Omega,\mathcal F,\mathbb P)\to(S_i,\Sigma_i)$ be random elements on a
common probability space. For each $i$, write

$$\sigma(X_i):=\{X_i^{-1}(B):B\in\Sigma_i\}\subseteq\mathcal F.$$

The family $(X_i)_{i\in I}$ is **independent** when the sigma-algebras
$(\sigma(X_i))_{i\in I}$ are independent in the sense of
[[def-independent-sigma-algebras-and-events]].

When $\Sigma_i$ is a Borel sigma-algebra, this agrees with the notation
$\sigma(X_i)$ from [[def-sigma-algebra-generated-by-a-function]].

Let $n\ge1$, and let
$X_i:(\Omega,\mathcal F,\mathbb P)\to(S_i,\Sigma_i)$ for $i<n$ be independent
random elements. Define

$$X=(X_0,\dots,X_{n-1}):\Omega\to\prod_{i<n}S_i.$$

Then $X$ is a random element of
$\left(\prod_{i<n}S_i,\bigotimes_{i<n}\Sigma_i\right)$, and its law is the
finite product of the marginal laws:

$$\mathbb P_X=\bigotimes_{i<n}\mathbb P_{X_i}.$$

A **measure kernel** from $(S,\Sigma)$ to $(T,\Tau)$ is a map $K:S\times\Tau\to[0,\infty]$ such that, for every $s\in S$, $A\mapsto K(s,A)$ is a measure on $(T,\Tau)$, and for every $A\in\Tau$, $s\mapsto K(s,A)$ is $\Sigma$-measurable. Measures and measurability have the meanings in [[def-measure]] and [[def-measurable-function-between-measurable-spaces]]; the evaluation functions use the Borel sigma-algebra on $[0,\infty]$.

A **probability kernel** satisfies $K(s,T)=1$ for every s. A **finite kernel** satisfies $K(s,T)<\infty$ for every s; there need not be a common bound on these masses. A **uniformly sigma-finite kernel**, in the convention of this page, comes with a specified sequence $T_n\in\Tau$ increasing to T such that $K(s,T_n)<\infty$ for every s and n. This is a common measurable exhaustion, not a bound uniform in s. A finite kernel has the constant exhaustion $T_n=T$. An arbitrary measure kernel is not assumed to have such an exhaustion.

All these requirements are pointwise in s, not merely almost everywhere for an unspecified measure on S. If T is empty, its only measure is zero, so a probability kernel into T can exist only when S is empty. If S is empty, the kernel requirements are vacuous. The zero kernel is finite. This definition selects no versions and uses no choice axiom.

Let $(X,\mathcal A)$ and $(Y,\mathcal B)$ be measurable spaces. Their
**product sigma-algebra** is

$$\mathcal A \otimes \mathcal B := \sigma(\{A \times B : A \in \mathcal A,\ B \in \mathcal B\}),$$

the sigma-algebra on $X \times Y$ generated by the measurable rectangles of
[[def-measurable-rectangle]].

For the empty family, put $\prod_{i<0}X_i:=\{()\}$ and define its **empty
product sigma-algebra** by

$$\bigotimes_{i<0}\mathcal A_i:=\{\varnothing,\{()\}\}.$$

For a nonempty finite family of measurable spaces $(X_i,\mathcal A_i)$ with
$i<n$, the **finite product sigma-algebra** is defined recursively by

$$\bigotimes_{i<1}\mathcal A_i := \mathcal A_0,\qquad \bigotimes_{i<n+1}\mathcal A_i := \left(\bigotimes_{i<n}\mathcal A_i\right)\otimes\mathcal A_n.$$

This recursive definition is the finite base case used later when the library
passes to countable product constructions.

Let $W$ be a subspace of a finite-dimensional inner product space $V$. For every $v\in V$, the vector $P_Wv$ is the unique point of $W$ nearest to $v$: for every $w\in W$,

$$\lVert v-P_Wv\rVert\le\lVert v-w\rVert,$$

with equality if and only if $w=P_Wv$.

Let $(v_0,\ldots,v_{r-1})$ be a finite linearly independent list in a real or complex inner product space. There is an orthonormal list $(e_0,\ldots,e_{r-1})$ such that, for every $k\le r$,

$$\operatorname{span}(e_0,\ldots,e_{k-1})=\operatorname{span}(v_0,\ldots,v_{k-1}).$$

It is obtained recursively from

$$u_k=v_k-\sum_{j<k}\langle v_k,e_j\rangle e_j,\qquad e_k=\frac{u_k}{\lVert u_k\rVert}.$$

For $r=0$, both lists are empty.

Let $n,d\in\mathbb N$ with $n,d\ge1$, and let $X\in\mathbb R^{n\times d}$ be a fixed design
matrix, and write $V_X:=\{X\theta:\theta\in\mathbb R^d\}\subseteq\mathbb R^n$
for its column space. For an observed vector $y\in\mathbb R^n$, the **fixed-design
least-squares fitted vector** is

$$\widehat\mu_X(y):=P_{V_X}y,$$

where $P_{V_X}$ is the orthogonal projection onto $V_X$, as defined in
[[def-orthogonal-projection]]. It is uniquely defined even when $X$ is rank
deficient. The nearest-point characterization in
[[thm-orthogonal-projection-is-the-unique-nearest-point]] says that
$\widehat\mu_X(y)$ minimizes $\|y-v\|_2$ over $v\in V_X$. This item defines the
fitted vector; it does not select a coefficient representation $\widehat\theta$.

Let $W$ be a subspace of a finite-dimensional inner product space $V$. The orthogonal-decomposition theorem ([[thm-finite-dimensional-orthogonal-decomposition]]) gives

$$V=W\oplus W^\perp$$

and associates to every $v\in V$ unique vectors $w\in W$ and $z\in W^\perp$ with $v=w+z$. The **orthogonal projection onto $W$** is the function

$$P_W:V\longrightarrow W,\qquad P_Wv=w.$$

Equivalently, $P_Wv$ is the unique vector of $W$ such that $v-P_Wv\in W^\perp$.

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ and $(Y,\mathcal B,\nu)$ be sigma-finite measure
spaces. Then:

1. the set function $E \mapsto (\mu \times \nu)(E)$ of
   [[def-product-measure-on-sigma-finite-spaces]] is a measure on
   $\mathcal A \otimes \mathcal B$;
2. for measurable rectangles,
   $$(\mu \times \nu)(A \times B)=\mu(A)\nu(B),$$
   with the nonnegative extended-product convention $0\cdot\infty=\infty\cdot0=0$;
3. the measure $\mu \times \nu$ is sigma-finite; and
4. it is the unique measure on $\mathcal A \otimes \mathcal B$ with the
   rectangle formula.

Let $\mathcal P$ be a pi-system on $X$. Then
$\lambda_X(\mathcal P)=\sigma_X(\mathcal P)$. Consequently, if $\mathcal D$ is
any lambda-system on $X$ with $\mathcal P\subseteq\mathcal D$, then
$\sigma_X(\mathcal P)\subseteq\mathcal D$.

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ be an arbitrary measure space. Let $f:X\to[0,+\infty]$ be measurable and define
$$\nu_f(A):=\int_A f\,d\mu \qquad (A\in\mathcal A).$$
Then $\nu_f$ is a measure on $(X,\mathcal A)$.

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ and $(Y,\mathcal B,\nu)$ be sigma-finite measure
spaces, and let $f : X \times Y \to [0,\infty]$ be product-measurable. Then
$x \mapsto \int_Y f_x\,d\nu$ and $y \mapsto \int_X f^y\,d\mu$ are measurable,
and

$$\int_{X \times Y} f\,d(\mu \times \nu) = \int_X \left(\int_Y f_x\,d\nu\right)d\mu = \int_Y \left(\int_X f^y\,d\mu\right)d\nu.$$

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ be an arbitrary measure space. Let $f_n:X\to[0,+\infty]$ be measurable for every $n\ge1$, with $0\le f_1\le f_2\le\cdots$, and suppose $f_n(x)\uparrow f(x)$ for every $x\in X$. Then
$$\int f_n\,d\mu\uparrow\int f\,d\mu.$$

derivations.claim: Write $\mathbf X=(X_1,\ldots,X_n)$ and $\epsilon_i=Y_i-g_0(X_i)$. For fixed $\mathbf x$, set $\kappa_1=\kappa(x_1,\cdot)$ and, for $1\le m<n$, apply [F10] to $\kappa_m$ and $\kappa(x_{m+1},\cdot)$ to obtain $\kappa_{m+1}$; both factors are probability measures, so the rectangle formula gives total mass one at each stage. Induction gives the finite product probability measure $\kappa_n(\mathbf x,\cdot)$ with rectangle values $\kappa_n(\mathbf x,\prod_iB_i)=\prod_i\kappa(x_i,B_i)$. The response rectangles form a pi-system because intersections of rectangles are rectangles, and [F5] says they generate the response product sigma-algebra. On response rectangles the evaluation is Borel in $\mathbf x$ by [F4] and [F10]. Because $\kappa_n(\mathbf x,\cdot)$ is a probability measure, the class of sets with Borel evaluation contains the whole space, is closed under complements by subtraction from $1$, and is closed under disjoint countable unions by limits of partial sums; [F11] therefore gives measurability for every response Borel set. For rectangles $A=\prod_iA_i$ and $B=\prod_iB_i$, iid sampling gives $P(\mathbf X\in A,\mathbf Y\in B)=\prod_i\int_{A_i}\kappa(x,B_i)P_X(dx)$, and repeated Tonelli [F13] gives $\int_A\kappa_n(\mathbf x,B)P_X^{\otimes n}(d\mathbf x)=\prod_i\int_{A_i}\kappa(x,B_i)P_X(dx).$ For each fixed response rectangle $B$, the left side of the target identity is a finite measure in $A$; the right side is also a measure by [F12], applied to the nonnegative measurable function $\mathbf x\mapsto\kappa_n(\mathbf x,B)$. Design rectangles form a pi-system because intersections are rectangles and generate the design product sigma-algebra by [F5], so [F11] extends the equality to every design Borel $A$. For each such $A$, both sides are finite measures in $B$: countable additivity on the right follows from countable additivity of $\kappa_n(\mathbf x,\cdot)$ and monotone convergence [F14], and their common total mass is $P_X^{\otimes n}(A)$ because the joint design marginal is $P_X^{\otimes n}$ and $\kappa_n$ is a probability kernel. Thus the response sets $B$ for which the identity holds for every $A$ form a Dynkin system (complements use the common total mass); they contain the response rectangles, so [F11] gives equality for every response Borel set. Under this product law the residuals are conditionally independent, have conditional means zero by [A2], and conditional second moments at most $\Delta$. Let $Q=\Pi_{\operatorname{col}(D)}$. The matrix $Q$ is a Borel function of $D$: partition the finite-dimensional matrix space by rank and, within each positive-rank stratum, by the lexicographically first nonzero maximal minor; on each resulting Borel piece, the corresponding independent columns form a matrix $C$. The Gram matrix $C^TC$ is positive definite, and $C(C^TC)^{-1}C^T$ is symmetric, idempotent, and has image $\operatorname{col}(C)=\operatorname{col}(D)$, so it is the orthogonal projection; at rank zero put $Q=0$. For any $v$, $UU^Tv$ belongs to $\operatorname{col}(D)$ and $U^T(v-UU^Tv)=0$, so its residual is orthogonal to the columns of $U$ and hence to $\operatorname{col}(D)$. The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> ([[def-choice-function]]).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

Let $(\Omega,\mathcal F,\mathbb P)$ be a probability space, let $n,K\ge1$, and let $Z_i=(X_i,Y_i)$, $1\le i\le n$, be iid random elements of $([a,b]\times\mathbb R,\mathcal B([a,b])\otimes\mathcal B(\mathbb R))$. Write $P_X$ for the law of $X_1$ and suppose the one-observation law is $P_X(dx)\kappa(x,dy)$ for a supplied Borel probability kernel $\kappa$ from $([a,b],\mathcal B([a,b]))$ to $(\mathbb R,\mathcal B(\mathbb R))$. Assume a Borel function $g_0:[a,b]\to\mathbb R$ is supplied such that, for $P_X$-almost every $x$, $\int |y|\,\kappa(x,dy)<\infty$, $g_0(x)=\int y\,\kappa(x,dy)$, and $\int (y-g_0(x))^2\,\kappa(x,dy)\le\Delta$ for a finite $\Delta\ge0$. Let $p_K:[a,b]\to\mathbb R^K$ be a fixed Borel $K$-dimensional spline basis and assume a deterministic $\bar\beta_K\in\mathbb R^K$, a constant $C\ge0$, and $\gamma>0$ satisfy
$$\int_{[a,b]}\{g_0(x)-p_K(x)^T\bar\beta_K\}^2\,P_X(dx)\le C^2K^{-2\gamma}.$$
Then, with the fitted training vector $\widehat{\mathbf g}_K$ from [[def-series-spline-least-squares]] and $\mathbf g_0=(g_0(X_1),\ldots,g_0(X_n))^T$,
$$E\left[\frac1n\|\widehat{\mathbf g}_K-\mathbf g_0\|_2^2\right]\le\frac{\Delta K}{n}+C^2K^{-2\gamma}.$$
This is expected empirical training-design loss.

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $p\in\mathbb N_0$, $0\le l\le p$, and $1\le q\le\infty$. Let $\mathcal T$ be a nonempty family of clamped degree-$p$ knot meshes on $[a,b]$, and let $(Q_\xi)_{\xi\in\mathcal T}$ be a mesh-uniform bounded local quasi-interpolant family as in [[def-local-spline-quasi-interpolant]], with common constants $M$ and $C_Q$. Fix $\xi\in\mathcal T$, write $Q=Q_\xi$, and let $f\in W^{l+1,q}(a,b;\mathbb R)$ with its continuous Sobolev representative. For each nonempty cell $I_m$ of $\xi$, let $J_m$ be its corresponding neighborhood and let $h_m$ be the largest cell length in $J_m$. Then
$$\|f-Qf\|_{L^q(I_m)}\le (1+C_Q)\frac{M^{l+1}}{l!}h_m^{l+1}\|D^{l+1}f\|_{L^q(J_m)}.$$
Writing $h=\max_m h_m$, the global bound is
$$\|f-Qf\|_{L^q([a,b])}\le (1+C_Q)\frac{M^{l+1+1/q}}{l!}h^{l+1}\|D^{l+1}f\|_{L^q([a,b])},$$
where $1/q=0$ for $q=\infty$. In particular, on a uniform mesh with interior knots of multiplicity $p+1$, the cellwise $L^2$ projector onto $\mathcal P_p$ is a local quasi-interpolant and gives the order-$h^s$ approximation bound for every integer $1\le s\le p+1$.

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $X,Y$ be real random variables on a probability
space, with $\mathbb E|Y|<\infty$, and choose a regular conditional law
$Q(x,dy)$ of $Y$ given $X=x$. On
$D=\{x:\int |y|\,Q(x,dy)<\infty\}$ define
$m(x)=\int y\,Q(x,dy)$, and put $m(x)=0$ off $D$. By
[[cor-conditional-expectation-as-a-measurable-function-of-the-conditioning-variable]],
$m$ is Borel measurable and $m(X)$ is a version of
$\mathbb E[Y\mid\sigma(X)]$. A **regression target** is the resulting
$P_X$-almost-sure equivalence class; a **chosen regression-function version**
is the particular Borel function selected by the specified conditional law.

Pointwise smoothness is an additional hypothesis on the chosen version. It is
not implied by existence of conditional expectation, and statements about
$m(x)$ at a specified point use that selected version.

Let $p\in\mathbb N_0$, $n\ge p+1$, and $a<b$. A clamped knot vector is a nondecreasing finite sequence
$$\xi_1=\cdots=\xi_{p+1}=a<\xi_{p+2}\le\cdots\le\xi_n<\xi_{n+1}=\cdots=\xi_{n+p+1}=b,$$
with $\xi_j<\xi_{j+p+1}$ for every $1\le j\le n$. Empty interior ranges are omitted. The multiplicity $\mu(\eta)$ of an interior knot $\eta$ is its number of occurrences among $\xi_{p+2},\ldots,\xi_n$.

Write $\mathcal P_p$ for the real polynomials of degree at most $p$. The degree-$p$ spline space $S_{p,\xi}$ consists of functions that restrict to a member of $\mathcal P_p$ on each nonempty knot interval and whose derivatives through order $p-\mu(\eta)$ agree across each interior knot $\eta$. The convention $C^{-1}$ means that no matching condition is imposed. For this piecewise definition, take knot cells left-closed and right-open; at a knot with no matching condition, the value is the one from the cell on its right, and at $b$ use the left limit. Thus the function value at a discontinuous knot is specified.

For each degree $d\in\{0,\ldots,p\}$, the functions $B_{j,d,\xi}$ are indexed by $1\le j\le n+p-d$. Set
$$B_{j,0,\xi}(x)=\mathbf 1_{[\xi_j,\xi_{j+1})}(x),\qquad 1\le j\le n+p.$$
For $1\le d\le p$ and $1\le j\le n+p-d$, define recursively
$$B_{j,d,\xi}(x)=\frac{x-\xi_j}{\xi_{j+d}-\xi_j}B_{j,d-1,\xi}(x)+\frac{\xi_{j+d+1}-x}{\xi_{j+d+1}-\xi_{j+1}}B_{j+1,d-1,\xi}(x),$$
where a term with zero denominator is defined to be zero. For every degree $d$ and every allowed index $j$, set $B_{j,d,\xi}(b)$ equal to its left limit. In particular, the degree-$p$ family has indices $1\le j\le n$. Its basis and regularity properties are proved in [[thm-spline-polynomial-reproduction]].

Let $p\in\mathbb N_0$ and let $\xi$ be a clamped knot vector as in [[def-b-spline-space-and-basis]]. The recursively defined degree-$p$ B-splines are nonnegative, are supported on $[\xi_j,\xi_{j+p+1}]$, and are piecewise polynomials of degree at most $p$. At a knot of multiplicity $\mu\le p$, each B-spline is $C^{p-\mu}$; multiplicity $p+1$ imposes no continuity requirement. Globally, the $n$ B-splines form a basis of $S_{p,\xi}$. In particular, every $q\in\mathcal P_p$ has a unique expansion $q=\sum_{j=1}^n c_jB_{j,p,\xi}$ on $[a,b]$.

On every nonempty knot interval $[\xi_m,\xi_{m+1})$, the active functions $B_{m-p,p,\xi},\ldots,B_{m,p,\xi}$ form a basis of $\mathcal P_p$ and sum to one. Globally, the $n$ B-splines form a basis of $S_{p,\xi}$. In particular, every $q\in\mathcal P_p$ has a unique expansion $q=\sum_{j=1}^n c_jB_{j,p,\xi}$ on $[a,b]$.

Fix a bounded interval $[a,b]$, a degree $p\in\mathbb N_0$, an exponent $1\le q\le\infty$, an integer $0\le l\le p$, and a nonempty family $\mathcal T$ of clamped degree-$p$ knot meshes on $[a,b]$. A **mesh-uniform bounded local quasi-interpolant** is a family of real-linear maps $Q_\xi:C([a,b];\mathbb R)\to S_{p,\xi}$, one for each $\xi\in\mathcal T$, for which there are common constants $M\in\mathbb N$ and $0\le C_Q<\infty$ such that the following hold for every $\xi\in\mathcal T$ and every nonempty cell $I_m$ of its mesh: there is a neighborhood $J_{\xi,m}\subseteq[a,b]$ containing $I_m$ and formed from at most $M$ adjacent knot cells; each point of $[a,b]$ belongs to at most $M$ of the neighborhoods $J_{\xi,m}$; (i) if $f=g$ almost everywhere on $J_{\xi,m}$, then $Q_\xi f=Q_\xi g$ almost everywhere on $I_m$; (ii) $Q_\xi v=v$ for every $v\in\mathcal P_l$; and (iii) $\|Q_\xi f\|_{L^q(I_m)}\le C_Q\|f\|_{L^q(J_{\xi,m})}$. The constants $M$ and $C_Q$ are independent of $\xi$. The derivative and continuous-representative conventions for Sobolev inputs are those of [[def-sobolev-space-wkp-and-its-norm]] and [[cor-one-dimensional-w-one-p-functions-have-absolutely-continuous-representatives]].

For a fixed mesh, the coefficient-functional formulation in Lyche–Manni–Speleers is one sufficient way to obtain these local stability and reproduction properties. Uniform constants in that construction give a family as defined here; this definition records the operator hypotheses used in the approximation proof.

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $p\in\mathbb N_0$, $0\le l\le p$, and $1\le q\le\infty$. Let $\mathcal T$ be a nonempty family of clamped degree-$p$ knot meshes on $[a,b]$, and let $(Q_\xi)_{\xi\in\mathcal T}$ be a mesh-uniform bounded local quasi-interpolant family as in [[def-local-spline-quasi-interpolant]], with common constants $M$ and $C_Q$. Fix $\xi\in\mathcal T$, write $Q=Q_\xi$, and let $f\in W^{l+1,q}(a,b;\mathbb R)$ with its continuous Sobolev representative. For each nonempty cell $I_m$ of $\xi$, let $J_m$ be its corresponding neighborhood and let $h_m$ be the largest cell length in $J_m$. Then
$$\|f-Qf\|_{L^q(I_m)}\le (1+C_Q)\frac{M^{l+1}}{l!}h_m^{l+1}\|D^{l+1}f\|_{L^q(J_m)}.$$
Writing $h=\max_m h_m$, the global bound is
$$\|f-Qf\|_{L^q([a,b])}\le (1+C_Q)\frac{M^{l+1+1/q}}{l!}h^{l+1}\|D^{l+1}f\|_{L^q([a,b])},$$
where $1/q=0$ for $q=\infty$. In particular, on a uniform mesh with interior knots of multiplicity $p+1$, the cellwise $L^2$ projector onto $\mathcal P_p$ is a local quasi-interpolant and gives the order-$h^s$ approximation bound for every integer $1\le s\le p+1$.

Assume the Axiom of Choice for the ACL and absolutely-continuous
fundamental-theorem interfaces. Let $I\subseteq\mathbb R$ be a nonempty open
interval, let $1\le p\le\infty$, let $\mathbb K\in\{\mathbb R,\mathbb C\}$,
and let $u\in W^{1,p}(I;\mathbb K)$, with weak derivative class $Du$. Then
there is exactly one continuous representative $u^*$ of the class of $u$ on
$I$ that is locally absolutely continuous, that is, absolutely continuous on
every compact interval contained in $I$, and satisfies
$$u^*(x)-u^*(y)=\int_y^xDu(t)\,dt\qquad\text{for every }x,y\in I,$$
where for $x<y$ the right-hand side denotes $-\int_x^yDu$, equivalently
$u^*(y)-u^*(x)=\int_x^yDu$ whenever $x\le y$.

If $I=(a,b)$ has finite endpoints, then $Du\in L^1(a,b)$, the representative
$u^*$ extends uniquely to an absolutely continuous function on $[a,b]$, and
the extension satisfies
$$u^*(x)=u^*(a)+\int_a^xDu(t)\,dt\qquad\text{for every }x\in[a,b].$$

The scalar field is arbitrary, $p=1$ and $p=\infty$ are included, and the
one-dimensional interval may be bounded or unbounded. The Axiom of Choice is
used only through the Countable-Choice and Dependent-Choice hypotheses of the
cited characterisation, fundamental-theorem and completeness interfaces.

derivations.claim: Use the disjoint cells $I_j=[t_j,t_{j+1})$, $0\le j<J$, with the final cell also containing $1$, and put $J_j=I_j$. For any continuous input $g$ and $x\in[t_j,t_{j+1}]$, $I_hg(x)=\frac{t_{j+1}-x}{h}g(t_j)+\frac{x-t_j}{h}g(t_{j+1})$. The nonnegative weights sum to one. Continuity makes the endpoint values limits from within $I_j$ and gives $\|g\|_{L^\infty(I_j)}=\max_{[t_j,t_{j+1}]}|g|$, so $\|I_hg\|_{L^\infty(I_j)}\le\|g\|_{L^\infty(J_j)}$. Continuous inputs agreeing almost everywhere on $J_j$ agree on its closure and hence have the same interpolant on $I_j$. The map is real-linear, reproduces every affine function, and is a continuous piecewise-linear spline by [F1]. Each neighborhood is one cell and each point belongs to exactly one neighborhood. Thus, as $J$ varies, the maps $I_h$ form a mesh-uniform family as in [F2] with $p=l=1$, $q=\infty$, $M=1$, and $C_Q=1$.

Let $M_2=\|D^2f\|_{L^\infty(0,1)}$. On a cell $[u,v]$ of length $h$, put $a_x=x-u$ and $b_x=v-x$. By [F3] applied to $f$ and $Df$, let $f^*$ and $g^*$ be their absolutely continuous representatives; $(g^*)'=D^2f$ almost everywhere and $f^*(x)-f^*(u)=\int_u^xg^*(s)\,ds$. The absolutely continuous function $t\mapsto(x-t)g^*(t)$ has derivative $-g^*(t)+(x-t)D^2f(t)$ almost everywhere, so the fundamental theorem for absolutely continuous functions gives $f^*(x)=f^*(u)+a_xg^*(u)+\int_u^x(x-t)D^2f(t)\,dt$, and the same formula at $v$. Since $I_hf(x)=f^*(u)+(a_x/h)(f^*(v)-f^*(u))$, subtraction and simplification yield $f^*(x)-I_hf(x)=-\int_u^x\frac{b_x(t-u)}hD^2f(t)\,dt-\int_x^v\frac{a_x(v-t)}hD^2f(t)\,dt$. Hence $|f^*(x)-I_hf(x)|\le M_2\{b_xa_x^2/(2h)+a_xb_x^2/(2h)\}=M_2a_xb_x/2\le M_2h^2/8$, since $a_x+b_x=h$ and $a_xb_x\le h^2/4$. This holds on every cell and at every point, so taking the supremum gives $\|f-I_hf\|_{L^\infty(0,1)}\le h^2\|D^2f\|_{L^\infty(0,1)}/8$.

Let $n,K\ge1$, let $p_K(x)=(s_1(x),\ldots,s_K(x))^T$ be a specified $K$-dimensional spline basis on the data domain, and let $(X_i,Y_i)_{i=1}^n$ be observed real-valued data with inputs in that domain. In particular, one may specify the degree-$p$ B-spline basis $p_K(x)=(B_{1,p,\xi}(x),\ldots,B_{K,p,\xi}(x))^T$. Form the design matrix $P\in\mathbb R^{n\times K}$ with row $p_K(X_i)^T$. The **series least-squares fitted training vector** is
$$\widehat{\mathbf g}_K=\Pi_{\operatorname{col}(P)}\mathbf Y,$$
the orthogonal projection of $\mathbf Y=(Y_1,\ldots,Y_n)^T$ onto the column space of $P$. Conditional on the realized design, this is the fixed-design least-squares fitted vector of [[def-fixed-design-projection-estimator]]. Equivalently, it is $P\widehat\beta$ for any minimizer $\widehat\beta$ of $\|\mathbf Y-P\beta\|_2^2$; all such minimizers have the same fitted training vector. The training prediction loss relative to a specified target vector $\mathbf g_0=(g_0(X_1),\ldots,g_0(X_n))^T$ is $n^{-1}\|\widehat{\mathbf g}_K-\mathbf g_0\|_2^2$. This definition specifies training fitted values and makes no test-risk assertion.

Let $(\Omega,\mathcal F,\mathbb P)$ be a probability space, let $n,K\ge1$, and let $Z_i=(X_i,Y_i)$, $1\le i\le n$, be iid random elements of $([a,b]\times\mathbb R,\mathcal B([a,b])\otimes\mathcal B(\mathbb R))$. Write $P_X$ for the law of $X_1$ and suppose the one-observation law is $P_X(dx)\kappa(x,dy)$ for a supplied Borel probability kernel $\kappa$ from $([a,b],\mathcal B([a,b]))$ to $(\mathbb R,\mathcal B(\mathbb R))$. Assume a Borel function $g_0:[a,b]\to\mathbb R$ is supplied such that, for $P_X$-almost every $x$, $\int |y|\,\kappa(x,dy)<\infty$, $g_0(x)=\int y\,\kappa(x,dy)$, and $\int (y-g_0(x))^2\,\kappa(x,dy)\le\Delta$ for a finite $\Delta\ge0$. Let $p_K:[a,b]\to\mathbb R^K$ be a fixed Borel $K$-dimensional spline basis and assume a deterministic $\bar\beta_K\in\mathbb R^K$, a constant $C\ge0$, and $\gamma>0$ satisfy
$$\int_{[a,b]}\{g_0(x)-p_K(x)^T\bar\beta_K\}^2\,P_X(dx)\le C^2K^{-2\gamma}.$$
Then, with the fitted training vector $\widehat{\mathbf g}_K$ from [[def-series-spline-least-squares]] and $\mathbf g_0=(g_0(X_1),\ldots,g_0(X_n))^T$,
$$E\left[\frac1n\|\widehat{\mathbf g}_K-\mathbf g_0\|_2^2\right]\le\frac{\Delta K}{n}+C^2K^{-2\gamma}.$$
This is expected empirical training-design loss.

Let $p\in\mathbb N_0$, $n\ge p+1$, and $a<b$. A clamped knot vector is a nondecreasing finite sequence
$$\xi_1=\cdots=\xi_{p+1}=a<\xi_{p+2}\le\cdots\le\xi_n<\xi_{n+1}=\cdots=\xi_{n+p+1}=b,$$
with $\xi_j<\xi_{j+p+1}$ for every $1\le j\le n$. Empty interior ranges are omitted. The multiplicity $\mu(\eta)$ of an interior knot $\eta$ is its number of occurrences among $\xi_{p+2},\ldots,\xi_n$.

Write $\mathcal P_p$ for the real polynomials of degree at most $p$. The degree-$p$ spline space $S_{p,\xi}$ consists of functions that restrict to a member of $\mathcal P_p$ on each nonempty knot interval and whose derivatives through order $p-\mu(\eta)$ agree across each interior knot $\eta$. The convention $C^{-1}$ means that no matching condition is imposed. For this piecewise definition, take knot cells left-closed and right-open; at a knot with no matching condition, the value is the one from the cell on its right, and at $b$ use the left limit. Thus the function value at a discontinuous knot is specified.

For each degree $d\in\{0,\ldots,p\}$, the functions $B_{j,d,\xi}$ are indexed by $1\le j\le n+p-d$. Set
$$B_{j,0,\xi}(x)=\mathbf 1_{[\xi_j,\xi_{j+1})}(x),\qquad 1\le j\le n+p.$$
For $1\le d\le p$ and $1\le j\le n+p-d$, define recursively
$$B_{j,d,\xi}(x)=\frac{x-\xi_j}{\xi_{j+d}-\xi_j}B_{j,d-1,\xi}(x)+\frac{\xi_{j+d+1}-x}{\xi_{j+d+1}-\xi_{j+1}}B_{j+1,d-1,\xi}(x),$$
where a term with zero denominator is defined to be zero. For every degree $d$ and every allowed index $j$, set $B_{j,d,\xi}(b)$ equal to its left limit. In particular, the degree-$p$ family has indices $1\le j\le n$. Its basis and regularity properties are proved in [[thm-spline-polynomial-reproduction]].

Let $p\in\mathbb N_0$ and let $\xi$ be a clamped knot vector as in [[def-b-spline-space-and-basis]]. The recursively defined degree-$p$ B-splines are nonnegative, are supported on $[\xi_j,\xi_{j+p+1}]$, and are piecewise polynomials of degree at most $p$. At a knot of multiplicity $\mu\le p$, each B-spline is $C^{p-\mu}$; multiplicity $p+1$ imposes no continuity requirement. On every nonempty knot interval $[\xi_m,\xi_{m+1})$, the active functions $B_{m-p,p,\xi},\ldots,B_{m,p,\xi}$ form a basis of $\mathcal P_p$ and sum to one. Globally, the $n$ B-splines form a basis of $S_{p,\xi}$. In particular, every $q\in\mathcal P_p$ has a unique expansion $q=\sum_{j=1}^n c_jB_{j,p,\xi}$ on $[a,b]$.

derivations.claim: On the clamped knot vector $(0,0,1,1)$, the only nonzero degree-zero spline on $(0,1)$ is $B_{2,0}=1$; the recurrence in [F3] gives $B_{1,1}=1-x$ and $B_{2,1}=x$, so $p(1/2)=(1/2,1/2)$. Therefore $p(1/2)^T\widehat\beta=(1/2,1/2)(0,2)^T=1$, the training residual and empirical training loss are zero, and the fitted vector equals the projection in [F1]. The chosen coefficient vector is one admissible representation of it.

The independent test squared error has expectation $E\{\widehat g(X')-g_0(X')\}^2=\int_0^1(2x-1)^2dx=\frac43-2+1=\frac13>0.$ Thus zero training loss does not imply zero independent test loss, consistent with the scope of [F2].

The example uses a single training observation and computes its fitted value in step 1.1.
The one-row two-column design is rank deficient; step 1.1 verifies the fitted projection while step 2.1 computes positive test risk.
Step 2.1 integrates the test error over the full closed support [0,1].
The coefficient (0,2) is supplied explicitly. Step 1.1 confirms it represents the unique training projection; the other possible coefficient fits are not selected by any family-choice assertion.

Positive test risk does not characterize this particular coefficient choice, and zero training loss is not asserted to determine off-design function values.

risk_review.notes: Read both steps and spline/least-squares/risk suppliers. Knots (0,0,1,1) give basis (1-x,x), the one-row design (1/2,1/2) times (0,2) is exactly 1 and hence attains the least-squares minimum zero.
